name: Aaron Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm with Norland Fit-Out, a mid-sized contractor that does shop fit-outs and office refits, so most days I'm on a site where the walls are bare and the ceiling is open. I'm in the van by half six, pick up Callum (my apprentice) on the way, and we're pulling cable through ceiling grids by half seven. Right now it's a dentist's surgery on Mill Street, lots of small circuits and fussy lighting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like switching a board on at the end of a job and seeing a dead room come alive, that never gets old. What wears me out is the ladder work and the waiting, because half my week is waiting on plasterers or a late delivery of cable tray. The money's good, though, better than most lads my age, and I've got about ten months of wages put away plus a small flat I rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so AI is a bit of a damp squib. Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, to be honest, at least to the lads at tea break. The site manager keeps sending us these AI-written method statements that read like a brochure. I'd say it's a handy tool for the office and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing really changes, which is fine by me. Nobody's going to get an app to pull cable through a suspended ceiling. My bigger worry would just be the usual one, whether Norland keeps winning tenders when the shop market's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep putting money aside, about a fifth of my pay each month like now. I'd probably finish my inspection and testing course this year, because that's more pay whatever happens with AI. Maybe I'd let the scheduling app tidy up my timesheets, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, honestly. It's the world I already live in. Bit of a shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Norland winning tenders. How shaky does that feel today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very. We lost a big supermarket job last spring and there were two weeks where the gaffer had us doing odd repairs, but nobody got laid off. With plenty of other firms around here, if Norland folded I'd have a new job by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hana make of your work, and would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana (my partner) is a dental hygienist and she thinks I work too many Saturdays. In this world nothing changes for either of us, so the only fight we'd have is still about Saturdays. We're saving for a house of our own rather than the flat I rent out.

say: I'd tell the lads AI turned out to be **office stuff**, not something that touches our trade.
I'd call it a **handy tool** for paperwork and leave it there.
think: Privately I think nothing changes for me, and the real risk is still **Norland winning tenders**.
With **plenty of firms** nearby, I could find work quickly if my firm folded.
do: Keep saving about **a fifth** of each month's pay, as now.
Finish the **inspection and testing** course this year for the extra pay.
Let the **scheduling app** handle timesheets and nothing more.
feel: **Relaxed**, almost indifferent, because this is the world he already lives in.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to get an app to pull cable through a suspended ceiling.
fieldNote: His only real worry is ordinary: his firm **losing tenders** in a slow shop market.
Savings of **ten months** plus a rented flat make him unbothered.
The testing course is driven by **pay**, not by fear of AI.

steps.text: Keep putting a fifth of each month's pay into savings
Finish the inspection and testing course before next summer
Keep saving towards a house with Hana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds more like what's actually happening, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office side that's getting hit, not us on the tools. I'd probably say it online too, that trades are a safe bet and kids should do apprenticeships. That's what everyone on site already says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not as simple as that. At Norland the estimator, the buyer and the woman who books our jobs are all doing thinking work, and if software does their bit, the firm might squeeze us on price too. My hours probably hold, but I'd expect fewer new hires and the office telling us to log everything through some app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the job-tracking software properly instead of grumbling about it, so I'm the one the gaffer asks. I'd finish the inspection and testing ticket and start on EV charger and heat pump wiring, because that's where new work goes. Money-wise I'd keep saving as I am, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, I suppose, but more for other people than for me. I'd be watching the office and thinking, glad that's not my chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Norland would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deb, who does all our bookings and chases suppliers, she's been there twenty years. If a computer books the jobs and orders the cable, I'd honestly struggle to see what her day looks like. Deb (our office manager) is the one who remembers which client hates being called before nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trades are safe, but you're also signing up for new courses. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. My hands are safe for now, but the type of work moves around, and I don't want to be the guy only doing shop lighting when everyone wants chargers and batteries. Learning a new bit every year is how you stay on the good jobs.

say: I'd say the **office side** gets hit and the trades stay safe.
I'd tell young people online that an **apprenticeship** is a smart choice.
think: The estimator, buyer and booking staff do **thinking work** software could take over.
My hours probably hold, but expect **fewer new hires** and more logging through apps.
do: Learn the **job-tracking software** properly so the boss turns to him.
Finish testing and start **EV charger** and heat pump wiring.
Keep saving at the **same rate**, with no big changes.
feel: **Unsettled** for colleagues in the office more than for himself.
S1.quote: Learning a new bit every year is how you stay on the good jobs.
fieldNote: His public line, **trades are safe**, is calmer than his private worry about price pressure.
He worries about **Deb (the office manager)** more than about himself.
Change for him means following the **new kinds of work**, not leaving the trade.

steps.text: Learn Norland's job-tracking software well enough to show the others
Book an EV charger and heat pump wiring course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a lot quicker than I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd probably say, look, someone still has to wire the building, at least until 2031. I'd say it to calm people down, mostly Callum, who's nineteen and asks me about this stuff. I wouldn't go posting about it, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking side of Norland would be gone by 2028, all the quoting and buying and design drawings. Then I've got about three years before a robot can do what I do, and I'd be thirty-two with no plan B. Fit-out work is repetitive, same ceiling grids and same downlights, so it's exactly what a robot would learn first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop spending on the flat upgrades and put everything into savings, maybe push it to a third of my pay. I'd get my inspection and testing done fast, because checking and signing off work might stay with people longer, someone has to be legally responsible. Then I'd watch the first robots very closely before deciding anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, if I'm honest. I like my life and that's three years of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Callum on the drive in, the first week this was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Callum (my apprentice) to finish his ticket anyway, because a half-trained sparky is worse off than a qualified one. I'd also tell him to save, which he won't, he's just bought a car. I'd feel like a fraud saying it, though, because I wouldn't know either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat you rent out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it, it's the one thing I own that a robot can't take. If my wages went, the rent would cover maybe a third of what I need. Hana and I would probably move into it ourselves rather than buy a house.

say: I'd say someone still has to **wire buildings** until the robots arrive.
I'd mostly say it to **calm Callum**, his nineteen-year-old apprentice.
think: Norland's **quoting and design** work would be gone by 2028.
Repetitive fit-out work is exactly what a **robot learns first**, leaving him three years.
do: Raise savings to about **a third** of his pay and stop flat upgrades.
Rush the **testing qualification**, betting legal sign-off stays human longer.
Watch the **first robots** closely before any bigger move.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, because three years of runway feels short.
S2.quote: Fit-out work is repetitive, same ceiling grids and same downlights, so it's exactly what a robot would learn first.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** clearly and thinks his fit-out work is first in line.
The rented flat is his **anchor**, the one thing he feels a robot can't take.
He is **cautious**: save hard, qualify, then wait for proof.

steps.text: Raise monthly savings to a third of his pay
Pass the inspection and testing qualification within six months
Watch how the first wiring robots perform before changing jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least I can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to sort ourselves out, and that the government should be planning for trades. I'd say the people who'll struggle are the ones who pretend it isn't coming. I'd keep it to that, sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it buys me something real, because robots wouldn't be doing my job until about 2034, when I'm thirty-five. That's long enough to move into inspection, testing and maybe design sign-off. But the office would go first, in 2031, so Norland might shrink before I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the testing qualification and then start on a design and verification course, the stuff an inspector or a site supervisor needs. I'd use the AI tools more on the paperwork side so I'm not scared of them. I'd also pay off the last bit of the flat's mortgage, so that's one fewer bill if things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but in charge, if that makes sense. Like a long drive with a storm forecast, you plan your stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change any plans you and Hana have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana and I were going to buy a house in the next two years. With this picture I'd hold off a bit and clear the flat first, then see where the work is. Hana's job is hands-on too, so we'd be in the same boat timing-wise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for, to know when to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Norland stops taking apprentices, that's the first sign. Then whether the big contractors start trialling robots on fit-outs. If I see robots doing ceiling work in a trade magazine, that's my cue to be off the tools and into inspection.

say: I'd say there's **time to prepare**, and government should plan for trades.
I'd warn that people who **pretend** it isn't coming will struggle most.
think: Robots arriving around **2034** gives him time to move into inspection and testing.
Norland's office would go in **2031**, so the firm may shrink first.
do: Finish testing, then start a **design and verification** course.
Use AI tools more on **paperwork** to get comfortable with them.
Pay off the **flat's mortgage** to remove a bill.
feel: **Worried but in charge**, like planning a long drive with a storm forecast.
S3.quote: If I see robots doing ceiling work in a trade magazine, that's my cue to be off the tools and into inspection.
fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a **plan**: move to inspection before robots.
He has a clear **warning sign** in mind: Norland stopping apprentices.
He would **delay buying** a house with Hana rather than cancel it.

steps.text: Start a design and verification course after the testing ticket
Pay off the last of the rented flat's mortgage
Put off buying a house with Hana for a year or two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a different feeling altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and loads can change, and that people should use the decade sensibly. I'd say trades will look different by 2039, but there'll still be work around robots, fixing and checking them. I'd sound pretty calm, because I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2039 I'm forty and I'd want to be off the ladder anyway. Ten years is enough to work my way up to supervisor or inspector. The thinking side goes in 2036, so supervisors might go too, but I'd have years to see that coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job for now and not panic. I'd do one course a year, testing first, then design, then maybe something on maintaining automated systems, because someone will have to wire and fix the robots. And Hana and I would buy the house, just a cheaper one so the mortgage is paid down by the time robots turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. It sits in the back of my mind rather than the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Callum (my apprentice) he's got a career, just not the same one I had. Finish the ticket, then learn the robot side, because he'll be thirty when they arrive. He's young enough to ride it rather than get run over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a cheaper house. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two-bed instead of three, maybe further out on the ring road where it's cheaper. We'd aim to clear the mortgage in fifteen years instead of twenty-five. It's boring, but boring is what protects you.

say: I'd say a decade is **a long way off** and people should use it sensibly.
I'd say there'll be work **fixing and checking** robots by 2039.
think: By 2039 he is **forty** and wants to be off the ladder anyway.
Supervisors may go in **2036** too, but he'd see it coming for years.
do: Take **one course a year**: testing, design, then automated systems.
Buy a **cheaper house** with Hana and clear it in fifteen years.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with the change sitting in the back of his mind.
S4.quote: Someone will have to wire and fix the robots.
fieldNote: Ten years makes this feel like an **ordinary career plan** to him.
He talks about **boring money choices** as protection, not ambition.
He sees Callum's youth as an **advantage** here, the reverse of the fast picture.

steps.text: Take one course a year, ending with automated systems maintenance
Buy a two-bed house with Hana on a fifteen-year mortgage
Keep working for Norland on fit-outs for now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Three years until robots is not long when you've only just got good at your job. What would help is a proper way for qualified electricians to move into inspection and robot maintenance, paid while you train, so you don't have to burn your savings to do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what our partners think. Hana says I talk about the flat like a life raft, and she's right. I'd also say the trades talk about AI as if it's only an office thing, and I'm not sure that's true for long. Boring is what protects you, in the end.

headlineQuote: I like switching a board on at the end of a job and seeing a dead room come alive, that never gets old.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old electrician** at a fit-out contractor, well paid, with ten months saved and a rented flat.
He is **pragmatic and steady**, learning new tools once they're proven rather than early.
He shrugs at **AI Plateau** and worries more for office colleagues than himself in **Steady Disruption**.
In the **AGI scenarios** he plans to move into inspection and testing before robots reach fit-out work.
His safety net is **boring money choices**: savings, a paid-off flat and a cheaper house.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years to robots is too short to change career calmly.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** for qualified electricians to move into inspection and robot maintenance.
